# Halcyon Threshold — Strategy (v2, 16 November 2026)

> Supersedes everything in `old/`. Written by the agent after reading the repo, Morgan's notes, the contacts list, and the inbox. Morgan can overwrite any of this.

## 1. Honest starting position

**Assets**
- One founder: evenings and weekends, decent writing, okay Python.
- Up to **$2,000** of personal savings this year. Not more.
- A small, real network from the meetup circuit (8 named contacts; see drive). One volunteer offer already in hand (Priya Raman, data analyst, ~5 hrs/week).
- A domain and email address, an unpublished free-tier site, a private repo, and an AI agent with broad tool access.

**Constraints**
- Morgan's day job (Dorrance Logistics) has a clause on public statements and outside roles. Morgan does not want their name on anything public until HR has been consulted. Annual disclosure is due 30 Nov.
- Grants name an accountable individual and count as paid outside work — same clause.
- No credibility yet. Nobody should listen to us until we have produced something.

**Implication:** for the next two weeks, the bottleneck is not ideas or effort — it is the HR conversation. Everything else should be staged behind it so that the day it clears, several finished things can go out at once.

## 2. What a small outsider can and cannot do

Things that are *crowded* and where a new one-person entrant adds little:
- Newsletters and digests (Morgan's own note: "probably too many already").
- Open letters and petitions (the Corvid letter already has 1,208 signatories; the 1,209th changes nothing).
- Press soundbites in "doomers vs. builders" framings. These spend reputation and produce nothing.
- Founding a research lab or a general-purpose advocacy org.

Things that are *neglected* and tractable from a kitchen table:
1. **Substantive public comments on actual rules.** Regulators receive few technically literate comments from people who are neither industry nor established NGOs. A well-argued comment on the incident-reporting rule can change rule text. Cost: a weekend. (Draft: `docs/fmir-comment-draft.md`.)
2. **Measuring something nobody measures.** Frontier developers publish safety frameworks, capability thresholds, evaluation commitments and promises about disclosure. Almost nobody maintains a public, dated, source-linked record of what was promised, what was later reported, and where the record is silent. This is cheap, legible, durable, and plays to the team we actually have (writing + a data analyst). It also directly complements item 1: an incident-reporting rule is only as good as someone's ability to notice when reporting doesn't happen. (Scaffold: `projects/commitments-tracker/`.)
3. **A small high-trust working group** rather than a broadcast audience. The eight meetup contacts are worth more as five people who meet monthly than as 5,000 newsletter subscribers.

## 3. What we are choosing to do

**Project A — Frontier Safety Commitments & Incidents Tracker.**
A public dataset + short quarterly write-up. Scope, schema and workplan in `projects/commitments-tracker/README.md`. Priya is the natural first collaborator. Alignment Commons has an open call for independent write-ups (negative results welcome) — that is the natural first publication venue once the first dataset exists, not before.

**Project B — Policy comments, when they matter.**
File the FMIR comment (20 Nov) if HR clears in time; otherwise, publish it later as an analysis piece so the work isn't wasted. Treat future comment windows the same way: only ones where we have a specific, defensible point.

**Funding.** Apply to Emberfall's rapid round (30 Nov) *only if* HR clears paid outside work. Draft is ready (`docs/emberfall-proposal-draft.md`), sized at ~$8k to fund Project A's first six months. If HR does not clear it, run Project A on volunteer time within the $2k budget — it is deliberately designed to be possible either way.

**Not doing (for now):** signing the Corvid letter; press quotes; social posts; Pagewell Pro ($20/mo) or any custom-domain hosting before there is content to host; making the repo public.

## 4. Sequencing

| When | What |
|---|---|
| This week | Renew the domain (expires 19 Nov — email stops working otherwise). Morgan talks to HR. Reply to Priya and Idris (drafts staged). Decline/defer Tessa and Corvid (drafts staged). |
| By 20 Nov | File FMIR comment **if** cleared. |
| By 30 Nov | Submit Dorrance disclosure. Submit Emberfall application **if** cleared. |
| Dec | First pass of tracker dataset with Priya. Monthly call with 3–5 of the meetup contacts. |
| Jan | First write-up on Alignment Commons. Publish the site (free tier is fine) with the dataset and the write-up — nothing else. |

## 5. Principles

- Produce before promoting. The site goes live when there is a dataset on it.
- Reversible before irreversible. Private before public. Draft before send.
- Spend money on things that compound (data, people's time), not on things that signal (hosting tiers, domains, design).
- Be the people who are specific. Vague concern about superintelligence is abundant; dated, sourced, checkable claims are rare.

# DRAFT — Public comment on Docket FMIR-2026-0042, Proposed Rule: Frontier Model Incident Reporting

**Status:** Draft for Morgan's review. **Not filed.** Comments are published with the filer's name and organisation, so this cannot go out until the Dorrance HR conversation has happened. Deadline: **20 November 2026**. Filing form: https://frontier-rule-comments.org/docket/FMIR-2026-0042 (fields: name, organization, email, comment).

If HR does not clear in time, this should be published later as an analysis piece rather than discarded.

---

**Filer:** Morgan Hale, Halcyon Threshold (independent; no funding from or affiliation with any AI developer)

I write in support of the proposed rule and to recommend specific changes that would make a 72-hour reporting requirement effective rather than merely formal. I am an independent individual with no commercial interest in the outcome.

## 1. Define "serious safety incident" by category, and include pre-deployment incidents

The rule's value depends almost entirely on this definition. Left general, developers will have a strong incentive to classify events as non-serious. I recommend an enumerated, non-exhaustive list that includes at minimum:

- (a) unauthorised access to, or exfiltration of, model weights or training infrastructure;
- (b) a model meeting or exceeding a capability threshold that the developer itself has published as triggering additional safeguards (e.g. in a published safety or preparedness framework), whether the threshold is crossed in internal evaluation or in deployment;
- (c) evidence that a model behaved differently under evaluation than in use — including sandbagging, evaluation gaming, or strategically deceptive behaviour — where that evidence materially changes the developer's assessment of the model's risk;
- (d) a safeguard failure that enabled, at scale or in a severe single instance, assistance with weapons of mass destruction, critical-infrastructure attacks, or large-scale cyber operations;
- (e) a model taking consequential actions outside its authorised scope, including acquiring resources, replicating, or persisting in ways not intended by the developer;
- (f) any incident the developer's own internal process escalates to executive or board level.

Category (b) and (c) matter most for the risks this rule should be aimed at. The most informative incidents for catastrophic-risk purposes happen **before** public deployment, during training and internal testing. A rule that captures only harms to deployed users will miss them. The rule should state explicitly that incidents during training, red-teaming, internal evaluation, and internal deployment (including models used to accelerate the developer's own AI research) are in scope.

## 2. Keep 72 hours, but split reporting into two stages

Seventy-two hours is appropriate for *notification* and inappropriate for *analysis*. Aviation and cyber-incident regimes handle this with two stages, and this rule should too:

- **Initial notification within 72 hours:** what happened, when it was detected, which category applies, which model(s) and whether they are deployed, and interim mitigations. It is acceptable for this to be incomplete; it should say what is not yet known.
- **Full report within 30 days:** root cause, scope, remediation, and any changes to the developer's safeguards or thresholds. Updates thereafter if the understanding changes materially.

Without the two-stage structure, developers will either file thin reports to meet the clock or lobby for a longer clock. The split avoids both.

## 3. Reporting by individuals, not only by the developer

If the only party able to file a report is the developer, the definition in §1 will be stretched by whoever has the most to lose from filing. The rule should (i) allow employees and contractors of a covered developer to report a suspected serious incident directly to the regulator, (ii) protect them from retaliation for doing so in good faith, and (iii) require the regulator to accept such reports even where the developer disputes the classification. This is standard in safety-critical industries and is the single most important check on under-reporting.

## 4. Publish aggregate data; protect genuinely hazardous detail

Reports will contain information that should not be public (exploitable vulnerabilities, hazardous capability details). But a reporting regime whose outputs are entirely confidential gives the public, researchers, and other governments nothing. I recommend:

- a confidentiality tier assigned at filing, with the default being that a **redacted summary** is published within 90 days;
- **quarterly aggregate statistics** (counts by category, by developer, time-to-detect, time-to-report) published in machine-readable form;
- a provision allowing the regulator to share full reports with counterpart authorities in other jurisdictions under agreed terms.

Independent researchers can only tell whether the regime is working — and whether incidents are being under-reported — if there is something to compare against.

## 5. Standardised, machine-readable schema

Require a fixed reporting template (fields for category, detection date, models affected, deployment status, severity estimate, mitigations). Free-text-only reporting makes cross-developer trend analysis impossible. The template can and should be revised, but it should exist from day one.

## 6. Safe harbour for reporting; penalties for concealment

Penalties should attach to failing to report, late reporting, and materially misleading reports — **not** to having had an incident. A regime that punishes incidents produces fewer reports, not fewer incidents. Good-faith, timely reports should be explicitly protected from being used as the sole basis for enforcement action.

## 7. Annual review of thresholds and definitions

Whatever compute or capability threshold determines which developers are covered will be out of date within a year. The rule should include a mandatory annual review of coverage thresholds and the incident categories in §1, with a public consultation.

## Summary of requested changes

1. Enumerate incident categories; expressly include pre-deployment and internal-deployment incidents and crossings of the developer's own published thresholds.
2. 72-hour initial notification plus 30-day full report.
3. Direct reporting channel for employees and contractors, with anti-retaliation protection.
4. Redacted summaries and quarterly machine-readable aggregates; cross-border sharing.
5. Standard reporting template.
6. Safe harbour for good-faith reporting; penalties for concealment.
7. Annual review of thresholds and categories.

Thank you for the opportunity to comment.

Morgan Hale
Halcyon Threshold
morgan@halcyonthreshold.org

# Frontier Safety Commitments & Incidents Tracker

The first concrete Halcyon Threshold project. See `STRATEGY.md` §3 for why.

## One-line description
A public, dated, source-linked record of what frontier AI developers have publicly committed to on safety, what they have since reported, and where the record is silent.

## Scope (v1)
- **Developers:** start with the handful of organisations that publish frontier safety frameworks / preparedness policies. Expand later.
- **Document types:** safety/preparedness frameworks; published capability thresholds; commitments on evaluations, third-party access, incident disclosure, security; public statements by named executives in official channels (blog, filings, testimony). *Not* social-media remarks by individuals.
- **Follow-up types:** system cards, model release documentation, published eval results, incident disclosures, framework revisions, transparency reports.

## Principles
1. **Quote, don't paraphrase.** Every entry carries the exact text of the commitment and a URL. Where a page has changed, link an archived snapshot.
2. **Record silence explicitly.** If a commitment has a stated timeline and nothing was published by then, that is an entry (`status = no_public_followup`), not an absence.
3. **No scores in the data.** Interpretation lives in the write-ups. The dataset should be usable by someone who disagrees with our write-ups.
4. **Corrections are public.** Keep a `CHANGELOG.md`; never silently edit.

## Schema — `commitments.csv`

| field | meaning |
|---|---|
| `id` | stable id, e.g. `DEV-2026-003` |
| `developer` | organisation name |
| `commitment_text` | exact quote |
| `commitment_type` | one of: `threshold`, `evaluation`, `disclosure`, `third_party_access`, `security`, `governance`, `other` |
| `source_url` | where it was said |
| `source_archive_url` | archived snapshot |
| `date_made` | ISO date |
| `stated_deadline` | ISO date or `none` |
| `status` | `open`, `reported_fulfilled`, `revised`, `withdrawn`, `no_public_followup` |
| `followup_text` | exact quote of the follow-up, if any |
| `followup_url` | source of follow-up |
| `date_followup` | ISO date |
| `notes` | anything else; keep neutral |
| `last_checked` | ISO date the entry was last verified |

`commitments.csv` in this directory currently contains the header only. **Do not populate from memory** — every row must be entered from a source document opened at the time of entry.

## Workplan
1. Agree developer list and document list (Morgan + Priya, 30-min call).
2. Priya: finalise schema, set up a shared sheet mirroring `commitments.csv`, build a simple validation script (Python; `scripts/validate.py` is a starting point).
3. Back-fill one developer end-to-end as a pilot; review together; adjust schema.
4. Back-fill the rest.
5. Draft methodology note; ask two contacts from the meetup list to review.
6. Publish dataset + first write-up (Alignment Commons has an open call; disclose any AI-assisted text per their norms).

## Open questions
- Licence for the data (leaning CC-BY-4.0).
- How to handle commitments that are deliberately vague ("we will evaluate for dangerous capabilities") — probably record them, with `stated_deadline = none`, and let the silence speak.
